headline: Lower Naryn registers 71 new firms in nine months, 31 of them in Bazar-Korgon
dek: With 18 struck off, the net gain is 53 firms; the business census due on 30 November will show how many actually trade.
paragraphs: The Lower Naryn District administration said on Monday that 71 new firms were registered in the district between January and September this year, against 52 in the same months of 2025, a rise of about 37 per cent. About 18 firms were struck off over the same nine months, leaving a net gain of 53.

The figures come from Register of Firms entries passed to the district by the Ministry of Economy. Bazar-Korgon accounts for 31 of the new registrations and Tash-Kömür, the district seat, for 17. The other 23 are spread over smaller towns and villages. Iyık Janyl is a separate city and is not counted in the district total.

Most of the new firms are small and work in fruit and walnut processing and drying, repair workshops, building and haulage. Between them they declared about 520 jobs, or roughly seven each. The administration did not break the figure down by trade, and declared jobs are what an owner writes on the registration form, not a payroll count.

District head Alisher Kholmatov called the new firms "small firms doing ordinary work". Bekbolot Sherov, press secretary of the Ministry of Economy, confirmed that the figures match the register's entries for the district and said the ministry has no separate count of how many of the new firms have since begun trading.

Hamid Yusupov registered a walnut-cracking and drying shop in Bazar-Korgon in May. Registering as a company cost 600 som at Talasbank, he said, and the rest of the process took most of five weeks. "The walnuts come in October and November, and the dryer has to be ready before them," he said. He employs four people in the season and two the rest of the year. Until now he had sold nuts as an individual at the bazaar's northern rows.

Registration is not the same as operation, and Prof. Raisa Akmatova, an economist at Talas State University, urged caution. A firm can be registered and never trade, she said, and a trading stall can be missing from the register altogether. She added that the Territorial Statistics Office's census slip, which is required before any new registration until 30 November, may have brought forward some applications this autumn. That is her reading and the figures do not show it either way.

The census is the better test. The Territorial Statistics Office's first census of business entities, ordered by Executive Directive 2026/24, runs to 30 November and counts bazaar stalls and farms for the first time. The Office's director, Gulbarchyn Ryskulova, has not commented on the district figures. Her office will publish its own count of operating firms after the census closes, and for Lower Naryn it will differ from the registrations, probably by a wide margin.

Until then the nine-month figures say what was filed, not what is working. The 18 firms struck off show that some of the new entrants close within a year or two, and the district did not say how many of them were registered in 2025. Nor did it say how many of the 520 declared jobs were seasonal, a question that matters in a town whose trade peaks in the walnut weeks of autumn.
